Assassin's Creed went downhill after they annualized it, and exemplifies one of my problems quickly: innovations can't be passed along because by the time that a game comes out and the fans say "I like this," the next one is too far into production to implement the thing fans liked. The example here would be the automatic walking-and-talking in Revelations, which made the "follow X around the entire map" missions more bearable.

Even when the different studios aren't named, you hit points where a game may as well be its own IP. Assassin's Creed IV was a great game, best to bear the AC name in my opinion, but it really wasn't an Assassin's Creed game considering most of it was about pirates that don't care about no Assassins or Templars or their respective creeds.

But using the example of Assassin's Creed one last time, here's a worst case scenario for annualized series:

Ubisoft Montreal Knew that AC Unity was not ready - DSOG

In particular there's one sentence I'd like to point out:

...the team realized during the game’s late development stage that it was not ready yet, however it refused to delay it as that would have an impact on the future Assassin’s Creed titles.

The game wasn't delayed because they had a schedule to keep, and they didn't want to delay next year's game.

A game in an established series was released broken because they didn't want to delay the next year's game.

Adherence to a schedule directly conflicted with the quality of their product, in an industry where quality is everything. As you can probably tell from the majority of my post, I was an Assassin's Creed fan.I am no longer, and the only thing that Ubi could do to make me buy another AC game is discount it by at least 66%. Through annualization, they've devalued their brand to the point where the thought of buying the game at full price never crossed my mind.

I wouldn't wish that on any other IP.
